passage: In the village near Tumkur, Amma cut the ripe mango into pieces on a steel plate. Shankar, eleven, leaned close. "Lokesh got the big piece with the seed!" Lokesh, nine, grabbed it. "You got two pieces yesterday!" "And you slept later on Sunday!" "You got new chappals first!" Amma put down the knife. The boys were not looking at the mango anymore; they were looking at her, waiting to see whose side she would take. Shankar's voice cracked a little. "You always give him more." Amma looked at the two of them, their faces fierce, and understood it wasn't really about mango at all.

qa.q: What was Amma cutting on the steel plate?
qa.a: She was cutting the ripe mango into pieces.

qa.q: What does Shankar's cracked voice suggest he really wants?
qa.a: It suggests he feels hurt and less loved, and wants to know he matters to Amma as much as Lokesh does, not just a bigger piece of mango.

qa.q: What could Amma do at this turning point?
qa.a: Instead of weighing pieces, she could reassure each boy of her love and give each some time alone with her, which answers the real need.

qa.q: How might Lokesh see the mango fight?
qa.a: Lokesh probably feels he is the one treated unfairly, remembering Shankar's two pieces yesterday.

grounding: It shows two children keeping count of shares, bedtimes and new things and demanding exact equality, when underneath they need to know they matter equally.

passage: In their Melbourne flat, Valentina, eleven, stood at the fridge with a notebook. "Mei got a new phone case and I didn't. That's three things this month." Mei, nine, ran in. "You stayed up till nine-thirty on Friday! I had to sleep at nine!" "Because I'm older!" "You got the bigger slice of pizza!" Their father looked up from the stove. "Are you two keeping score?" Valentina held up her notebook proudly. It had columns: Mei, Me. He sat down at the table. "What would it mean if Mei got more?" Valentina's face changed. She said quietly, "That you like her more." Mei looked at her sister, surprised. "I thought you thought that about me."

qa.q: What columns did Valentina's notebook have?
qa.a: It had two columns: Mei and Me.

qa.q: What does Valentina's quiet answer reveal about her feelings?
qa.a: It reveals she is worried her father likes Mei more, so keeping score is really about feeling she matters.

qa.q: Why was the father's question a good turning point?
qa.a: Asking what it would mean if Mei got more helped Valentina say the real worry, so he can reassure both girls rather than count things.

qa.q: What does Mei's reply show about how she sees things?
qa.a: It shows Mei had the same fear, thinking she was the one who mattered less.

grounding: It illustrates siblings counting shares, bedtimes and new things and demanding exact fairness, when underneath each needs to know they matter as much.

passage:
It was forty-four degrees in Jodhpur, the power had gone, and there was exactly one mango left in the fridge.

Ammi cut it in two. Samir looked at his half, then at Kashish's.

"Hers is bigger!"

"It is NOT!"

"It is! Look, the seed side is mine!"

Kashish held hers up. "Fine, you got the seed. But you got the later bedtime last week. And the new school bag."

"You got the window seat on the bus to Nani's!"

Ammi put the knife down. They weren't really arguing about mango. They'd been keeping score for weeks: bedtimes, bags, seats, who got the first roti.

She sat down between them. "Do you both think I love the other one more?"

Neither answered. But both of them stopped chewing.

qa.q: How hot was it in Jodhpur?
qa.a: Forty-four degrees.

qa.q: What are Samir and Kashish really worried about underneath the mango argument?
qa.a: Both feel anxious that they might matter less than the other, so they keep score of every share.

qa.q: What does Ammi do that gets to the real issue?
qa.a: She sits between them and asks if they think she loves the other more, naming the feeling under the fairness counting.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel when Ammi asks her question?
qa.a: She may feel caught and a little relieved, since the question touches what she really worries about.

grounding: On a hot day Samir and Kashish fight over mango halves, bedtimes and seats, keeping score because each needs to know they matter as much.

passage:
When Jaya got a phone for starting Class 7, Indu, two years younger, counted everything.

"She got a phone. I didn't get anything."

"You'll get one in Class 7 too," Papa said.

"She also got to stay up till ten on Friday. I had to sleep at nine thirty."

"She's older."

"She got the bigger room. She got the new school shoes first. She got the front seat."

Jaya rolled her eyes. "And you got the bigger piece of cake on my birthday."

Papa looked from one to the other in their Pune flat. They had a list for everything.

That night, Indu said quietly to Mummy, "Do you like Jaya more?"

Mummy held her close. "I love you exactly as much. Not less, not more."

qa.q: What did Jaya get for starting Class 7?
qa.a: A phone.

qa.q: What was Indu worried about underneath all the counting?
qa.a: Whether she mattered as much as Jaya; she felt worried she was loved less.

qa.q: How did Mummy respond, and why was it right?
qa.a: She held Indu and said she loved her exactly as much, answering the real need beneath the list.

qa.q: How does Jaya see Indu's list?
qa.a: She finds it annoying and has her own list, showing she too is counting to be sure she matters.

grounding: Jaya and Indu count phones, bedtimes and cake, demanding equality, because underneath each needs to know she matters as much.

passage:
"Ammi, why does Hina get to stay up till nine thirty?"

"Because she's older, Rafiq."

"By one year!"

"Still."

"And she got the bigger slice of pizza."

"They were the same."

"No, hers had more cheese."

"Rafiq..."

"And when we went to the shop you bought her the red pencil box and me the blue one."

"You said you wanted blue."

"But hers was shinier."

Hina called from the other room: "He's counting again!"

"I'm not counting!"

Ammi sat down on his bed. "Rafiq, what's this really about?"

He was quiet. Then, very small: "Do you like her more?"

"No, jaan. Never. Come here."

qa.q: What colour pencil box did Rafiq get?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What was Rafiq really worried about?
qa.a: He was worried that Ammi liked Hina more, and he needed to know he mattered just as much.

qa.q: What did Ammi do that helped?
qa.a: She sat down and asked what it was really about, which let Rafiq say his real worry, and then reassured him.

qa.q: How does Hina see Rafiq's counting?
qa.a: She finds it annoying and teases him, saying he's counting again.

grounding: In dialogue Rafiq counts bedtimes, pizza and pencil boxes, demanding equality with his sister, until his mother reaches the worry that he matters less.

passage: Last year my sister Maryam and I kept a secret list on the back of the kitchen calendar. Who got the bigger piece of cake. Who sat in front. Who went to bed later. I even measured our milk glasses with a ruler. When Maryam got a phone for Class 7, I cried so much that Ammi couldn't talk to me. It wasn't really the phone. My friend Minakshi asked, "Zainab, would you even use it?" I said no. I just wanted to know I counted as much as Maryam. Then Ammi took me out alone for ice cream and said, "You'll never be the same as Maryam, and I'll never love you less." I tore up my half of the list after that.

qa.q: What did Zainab measure with a ruler?
qa.a: Their milk glasses.

qa.q: What was Zainab really feeling when Maryam got the phone?
qa.a: Zainab felt jealous and unsure of being loved as much; it was not really about the phone at all.

qa.q: What did Ammi do that helped?
qa.a: Ammi spent time alone with Zainab and said plainly that the two would never be the same but the love would never be less.

qa.q: How might Maryam have felt about the secret list?
qa.a: Maryam may have felt watched and tired of every piece of cake being counted, and caught up in the same contest.

grounding: Shows a child keeping exact score of shares and treats with a sibling, when the real need is to know of mattering just as much.
